input.question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?
input.ground_truth: I've always tied it to the invention of meiosis. Mitosis divides cells, but meiosis make half-cell kits, that can then combine in rapidly expanding numbers of ways. I see it as several billion years of mitosis and then meiosis gets discovered and boom: Cambrian Explosion.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have just one tiny Lego block. You can make more by copying that one block again and again, and soon you have a pile of the same kind of block. That’s like how the very first living things, called single-celled organisms, could make more of themselves by splitting in half.

But later, some of these tiny living things started working together in pairs, like two Lego blocks joining to make a bigger and better toy. When they work together, their “toys” (or babies) can be different and sometimes better at surviving. This is called needing a partner to make new life. It’s like having two different Lego sets and combining them to make something new and cool!

So, at first, one cell could make more by itself, but later, working with a partner helped make stronger and more varied living things. That’s why some creatures started needing a partner to have babies.
